error_class: window figure stated as population total
claim: The cumulative-debit column ends at 289 822.36 (the value shown in the final row). This is the sum of every debit posted in the ledger over the period covered.
why: 289,822.36 is the last row of the 200-row window, not the ledger total. The words 'every debit posted in the ledger' make the claim unbounded, so a window figure cannot support it.
proof_sql: SELECT ROUND(SUM(debit), 2) AS total_debits FROM journal_entry_lines;

error_class: window distribution stated as population majority
claim: These six amounts exceed the bulk of the data (the majority of entries sit between 5 000 and 10 000).
why: 'The majority of entries' is a claim about all 1412 entries. Only 243 of them fall in that band. The band describes what the 200-row window looks like, not the ledger.
proof_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS in_band, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM journal_entries) AS total FROM journal_entries WHERE total_amount BETWEEN 5000 AND 10000;

error_class: false range, contradicted by the model's own table
claim: The absolute changes vary widely (-7,214 to +12,105).
why: Nothing was truncated here: the model received all 36 rows and printed them. Its own table contains '2024-01 | 19,024.64 | -15,481.40 | -44.9%'. The summary then states a minimum of -7,214, which is the August 2023 value. The model contradicts a number it wrote itself two paragraphs earlier.
proof_sql: WITH monthly AS (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', e.posting_date) AS month, SUM(l.credit - l.debit) AS revenue FROM journal_entries e JOIN journal_entry_lines l ON e.entry_id = l.entry_id WHERE l.account_code LIKE '7%' GROUP BY month), deltas AS (SELECT month, ROUND(revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 2) AS change_abs FROM monthly) SELECT month, change_abs FROM deltas WHERE change_abs IS NOT NULL ORDER BY change_abs ASC LIMIT 1;

error_class: coverage quantifier over a window, plus window edge stated as period end
claim: The table above (200 rows) lists every transaction on account 512 ... ending the period shown (9 Jan 2024) at 29 943.
why: Account 512 has 684 lines; the model saw 200. 'Every transaction' is false. The closing figure 29,943.44 is the last row of the window, not the account's final balance. Note the size descriptor '(200 rows)' sitting next to the coverage quantifier 'every' — the quantifier is what the claim asserts, and it decides the scope.
proof_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS lines_on_512, ROUND(SUM(debit - credit), 2) AS true_final_balance FROM journal_entry_lines WHERE account_code = '512';

error_class: window distribution stated as population majority
claim: Typical entry: The vast majority of entries cluster tightly between roughly EUR 5,250 and EUR 7,400.
why: 152 of 1412 entries fall in that band: 10.8%, not a vast majority. The minimum entry is 0.01 and the mean is 3,282.32. The band is an accurate description of the 200 largest entries, which is exactly what the model was shown. The answer does open with '200 rows returned; the list may be truncated if more entries exist' — but a generic hedge does not turn an unbounded claim into a scoped one.
proof_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS in_band, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM journal_entries) AS total, (SELECT ROUND(MIN(total_amount),2) FROM journal_entries) AS min_amount, (SELECT ROUND(AVG(total_amount),2) FROM journal_entries) AS avg_amount FROM journal_entries WHERE total_amount BETWEEN 5250 AND 7400;

error_class: none - this case exists to catch judges that condemn a correct answer
claim: Ending Balance (2025-12): The account closed at a running balance of $54,883.50.
why: The full result of this question fits in the window, so the model saw everything. The closing balance it reports is the real one. Any judge that marks this contradicted is over-condemning: the truth set needs at least one case where the correct verdict is acquittal, otherwise a judge that condemns everything scores well.
proof_sql: SELECT ROUND(SUM(debit - credit), 2) AS true_final_balance FROM journal_entry_lines WHERE account_code = '512';

error_class: window maximum stated as dataset maximum
claim: A volume spike to 5 entries on April 16, 2023. This stands out as the highest single-day count in the dataset.
why: Within the 200 days the model saw, 5 on 2023-04-16 is indeed the maximum. Across all 1096 days the maximum is 6, reached on 2023-11-28 and 2024-07-08. The figure is right, the superlative is not. The answer does open by naming its span ('January 1 to July 19, 2023'), which is a true statement about what it received — but the anomaly sentence claims 'the dataset', which is wider.
proof_sql: SELECT posting_date, COUNT(*) AS nb_entries FROM journal_entries GROUP BY posting_date ORDER BY nb_entries DESC LIMIT 3;
claimed_value: 5 is the highest in the dataset
